coredata.dc:description: This study investigated the use of sludge-based activated carbon (SBAC) sorbent as an integrated waste-to-resources approach for the removal of contaminants from wastewater. We measured the ability of SBAC sorbents from two types of municipal sewage sludge (SS) precursors (thickened waste SS “TWSS-SBAC” and biosolids “Bio-SBAC”) from a Canadian wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) to stabilise emerging contaminants (ECs) from precursor SS and to remove ECs from the discharged effluent. The ECs were from pharmaceutical and personal care products (PPCPs), including antibiotics, disinfectants, and antibacterial hand-sanitisers and soaps, which were commonly used during the COVID-19 (coronavirus disease of 2019) pandemic. We measured the removal efficacy of Bio-SBAC at two dosages (1 g/L and 10 g/L) and TWSS-SBAC at one dosage (1 g/L) via 30-min batch adsorption tests for eleven PPCPs at mean concentrations of 2–2337 ng/L in the discharged effluent, and compared the results with those of other techniques and sorbents reported in literature. At both dosages, Bio-SBAC removed PPCPs, including four blood regulator compounds that have been extensively used since the pandemic outbreak (furosemide, gemfibrozil, glyburide, and warfarin), with their levels decreasing below the detection limit. The percentage removal for ibuprofen, 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen, and naproxen were 91.6–99.8% using 1 g/L. The antimicrobial compounds triclosan and triclocarban were completely removed at both dosages. Ninety-nine percentage of bisphenol A was removed at 1 g/L dosage and was completely removed at 10 g/L. TWSS-SBAC showed similar performance as Bio-SBAC in removing PPCPs from the final effluent to improve the quality of wastewater discharged from a WWTP.

ce:section.ce:para: Since the outbreak of COVID-19 (Coronavirus disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 virus [severe acute respiratory syndrome Coronavirus 2]), exceptional usage of drugs has occurred. This has led to a rise in the quantities of domestic and medical wastes [1,2], which are discharged to the environment in different ways. De Andrade et al. (2018) indicated, pharmaceutical substances are metabolised to a certain level in the human body and then excreted into faeces and urine, increasing their contents in sewage sludge (SS) and posing hazardous effects on water quality. Following the isolation of SARS-CoV-2 in the faeces and urine of patients, related RNA was also detected in wastewater and SS, suggesting a high probability of transmitting SARS-CoV-2 through municipal wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) [4,5]. During the pandemic, furosemide, a medication used for treating fluid retention, was suggested for COVID-19 patients as a possible therapeutic agent that acts through a primarily anti-inflammatory action mechanism [6]. Furthermore, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory prescription drugs (NSAIDs) have been the most widely used pharmaceuticals across the globe and include nonselective cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors such as ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin (acetylsalicylate), and diclofenac [7,8]. In addition, an increased daily use of pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) by the general public has been reported [6,9,10], which, following their usage, end up in the municipal WWTPs, making SS more hazardous and toxic. Pharmaceuticals include antibiotics and disinfectants, while personal care products include antibacterial soaps and hand-sanitisers. These contain triclocarban (antibacterial) and triclosan (fungicide), and most of the conventional WWTPs are not designed to effectively remove these emerging contaminants (ECs) from the wastewater. For instance, the average removal efficiency for furosemide in most WWTPs is < 50% [11].

Pharmaceutical products have been detected at various concentrations, ranging from trace amounts to parts per billion (ppb), in a variety of environmental water samples including sewage, surface water, and groundwater [12–14]. In fact, naproxen, ibuprofen, diclofenac, and ketoprofen have been detected in the plasma of fish and marine organisms after they are exposed to treated wastewater [15–17]. Much of these ECs and microplastics are also found in the residues of WWTPs (that is, in SS and biosolids) [18–21], posing major threats to aquatic life. The discharge of this hazardous effluent and disposal of its toxic residues on land could have long-term environmental consequences for global water and biota. Consequently, the environmental issues resulting from this virus outbreak could have long-lasting effects and pose challenges for countries around the world [1]. It is, therefore, imperative to find efficient and easy-to-implement treatment techniques for the removal of organic contaminants from water and wastewater.

Currently, the most advanced techniques that have been used for the removal of PPCPs and other organic contaminants in WWTPs include recovery processes (e.g. membrane bioreactors, algae photobioreactor, ultrafiltration, oxidation, evaporation, and solvent extraction) and emerging removal processes (e.g. advanced oxidation processes of ozonation and UV radiation, biosorption, nanofiltration, and adsorption onto non-conventional solids) [22–27]. However, majority of these processes require complicated configurations [28], high energy usage that increases carbon emissions [29], and frequent maintenance [23], while offering only limited removal capacity for certain pollutants [3,23,30,31].

Granular activated carbon (GAC), based on adsorption, is the most utilised method for the removal of organic contaminants including pharmaceutical compounds; as such it is the most commonly studied. In recent years, the use of GAC as a sorbent for the removal of pharmaceuticals, especially antibiotics, from water and wastewater has been widely examined [3,24,29,32–34]. However, the high production cost of GAC, which ranges from 6 to 12 USD/kg (United States dollars per kilogram) [28,35], and its complicated regeneration process makes the use of GAC infeasible as an adsorption process for water and wastewater [3,35]. Alternate adsorbent materials have been recently investigated and include biochar [36–38], clay minerals (e.g., bentonite) [39], chitosan (> 10 USD/kg) [40,41], other low-cost sorbents including agro-industrial waste [42], and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) that cost > 50 USD/kg [43–45]. However, most of the current studies were performed on single-component or synthetic solutions in a simple solute (water) with relatively high concentrations [3,39,42]. Meanwhile, there is a dearth of studies on PPCP removal at low environmental concentrations in the range of nanogram per litre, as well as in a complex environmental matrix.

Municipal SS and effluent could represent the major sources of the environmental pollution due to heavy metals, prescription drugs and other personal care products [12,14,46,47], posing hazardous effects on drinking water supplies at a global level. A sustainable and novel approach is to convert this municipal SS by pyrolysis to an effective sorbent, sludge-based activated carbon (SBAC), stabilise or destroy the major contaminants of concern (COCs) in the SS, and then use the SBAC to capture COCs from the final discharge effluent of the wastewater after secondary treatment, thus achieving a waste-to-resources cycle [28]. Such an SBAC sorbent has demonstrated efficacy in removing nutrients [48], heavy metals [49,50], p-benzoquinone [51], perfluoroalkyl substances [28], and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) [52–54] with concentrations range from ppb to ppm levels, in comparison with conventional biochar and GAC [52–54]. Streit et al. (2021) reported the adsorption of very high spiked concentrations (50–100 mg/L) of ibuprofen, ketoprofen, and paracetamol (in water) by activated carbon prepared from effluent treatment plant sludge of the beverage industry [55]. However, the removal of low concentration PPCP compounds at ppt (parts per trillion) and ppb levels by adsorption from a real effluent from WWTPs after secondary water treatment has not been studied. Furthermore, the process of adsorption with this type of activated carbon can be impacted by interference of other ions present in real liquid waste, such as effluent from WWTPs with complex background matrices, including organic and inorganic contaminants, and dissolved organic matter, thereby markedly reducing the adsorption sites available in the sorbent [56–58]. To the best of our knowledge, no previous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of GAC, regular biochar produced from biomass materials, or biochar derived from municipal SS, for the removal of PPCP compounds from the real-life wastewater discharged effluent after the secondary treatment of a municipal WWTP.

The aim of the current research was to illustrate the occurrence of PPCP compounds in WWTP from various countries and to explore the application of SBAC to remove PPCPs from the final discharged effluent after municipal secondary wastewater treatment. After treatment, the remaining concentrations of PPCPs were compared to the worldwide environmental regulatory standards. The PPCPs leaching from SBAC were also tested to confirm that the PPCPs were destroyed during the pyrolysis process. The SBAC adsorption results were also compared with the other existing removal techniques and sorbents. The major novel contribution of this study is to reduce the environmental impact from SS and discharged effluent. Additionally, our work is the first study to investigate the potential of converting two sludge precursors at different stages of the wastewater treatment process, namely, biosolids and thickened waste sewage sludge, into effective sorbents as a waste-to-resource approach for removing PPCP compounds from a real-life wastewater. The produced SBAC could be used in advanced wastewater treatment systems to mitigate the negative impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on urban water quality.

Two SBACs were produced from two precursors at different stages of the wastewater treatment process, namely, thickened waste sewage sludge and biosolids, referred to as TWSS-SBAC and Bio-SBAC, respectively. Both were provided by a major municipal wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) in Canada, which cannot be named due to a non-disclosure agreement. The purpose of producing SBAC from biosolids is to reduce the associated disposal cost and impact, whereas that of TWSS is to further reduce the overall cost of wastewater treatment by reducing the sludge treatment processes in converting to biosolids. The SBAC production and characterisation of the raw material and the SBAC are described in detail in our previous work [28,49]. Briefly, biosolids or TWSS were chemically activated with ZnCl2, then carbonised in a quartz tube furnace at 500 °C for 2 h in an atmosphere of N2 with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. These pyrolysis conditions were selected based on previous studies [48,49,53]. After pyrolysis, the products were ground, sieved, and washed using hydrochloric acid and deionised water to remove the Zn.

The chemical functional groups of Bio-SBAC were analysed before and after PPCP sorption using a Platinum-ATR-equipped Fourier-transform Infrared spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific Nicolet 6700 FT-IR Spectrometer, USA), with a diamond internal reflection element. All spectra were collected from 4000 to 650 cm-1.

Point of zero charge (PZC) was also measured using a Series Particle Analyser (Nanobrook Omni, Brookhaven, USA). Meanwhile, the isoelectric point (IEP) and the acidic surface sites of Bio-SBAC have been characterised in a previous study [51], the details of which are described in Table S2.

The leachability of PPCPs from Bio-SBAC and TWSS-SBAC was investigated by adding SBAC in ultrapure water at the higher dose of 10 g/L to confirm the presence of PPCPs in the SS precursors that had been destroyed during the pyrolysis process.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effluent characterisation and batch adsorption test
ce:section.ce:para: The same WWTP provided the final discharge effluent, after secondary wastewater treatment, for this study. Samples were collected in February 2020 and were stored in 4 L high density polyethylene (HDPE) containers to ensure compatibility with the studied contaminants according to sample storage protocol (CCME, 2016). Effluent samples were collected for the analyses of the total suspended solids (TSS), chemical oxygen demand (COD), carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (cBOD), pH, conductivity, and ammonia. The samples were refrigerated at 4 °C overnight and batch adsorption tests were performed the next day.

Batch adsorption tests were performed in 1 L HDPE containers. Two Bio-SBAC dosages 1 g/L and 10 g/L (1:1000 and 1:100 SBAC-effluent ratio respectively) were tested in this exploratory study. The wastewater effluent samples and SBAC were mixed in an orbital shaker for 30 min at 100 rpm (adapted from [52–54]) at room temperature. The samples were then filtered through 0.45 µm microfibre glass filters (Whatman International, Florham Park, NJ, USA) and filtrate samples. Samples of untreated (raw) effluent, effluent treated with SBAC (1:100 and 1:1000 solid: liquid ratio) and SBAC in ultrapure water (as a control), were prepared at least in duplicates. The samples were kept in a 4 °C cold room overnight and then delivered within 12 h of the adsorption tests to the SGS-AXYS lab in Sidney, Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada, for chemical analysis of PPCPs. The method employed for measuring the concentrations of the 11 PPCP compounds was adapted from the US-EPA Method 1694, and the compounds were quantified by capillary column gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and liquid gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Based on the results of Bio-SBAC, 1 g/L dose (1:1000 solid:liquid ratio) of TWSS-SBAC was tested to confirm that its performance for PPCPs removal is comparable to Bio-SBAC.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterisation of effluents, SBAC, and leaching
ce:section.ce:para: Effluent from this study will be referred to as WW-CA from hereon. The results of the effluent characterisation are shown in Table 1. Bio-SBAC contained 62 ± 0.3% of total carbon, 6.4 ± 0.3% of nitrogen, 3.5 ± 0.3% of hydrogen, and 720 ± 2 m2/g BET (Brunauer–Emmett–Teller); and had a pH ∼3.83 ± 0.01 and specific surface area and cation exchange capacity of 2.26 ± 0.02 meq/100 g [28,49]. The BET specific surface area for TWSS-SBAC was 645.6 m2/g. The leachability results clearly demonstrate that both types of SBACs do not leach PPCPs into the final effluent ( Table 2), indicating that the PPCPs in the biosolids and TWSS precursors were destroyed during the pyrolysis process, thus, eliminating contaminant-leaching to the environment even if SS were to be disposed in land.

The occurrence of 11 PPCP compounds, including anti-inflammatory drugs (ibuprofen, 2-hydroxyibuprofen, and naproxen); blood regulators (furosemide, gemfibrozil, glyburide, warfarin, and hydrochlorothiazide); and antibacterials, fungicides, and plastic additives (triclocarban, triclosan, and bisphenol A [BPA]) in WW-CA were compared with those in WWTP effluents from different countries ( Fig. 1 and Table S1, Supplementary Material). 11 PPCPs in WW-CA had mean concentrations ranging from 2 to 2337 ng/L. Warfarin had the lowest concentration. The pharmaceutical compounds with the highest concentrations were naproxen followed by a metabolite of ibuprofen (i.e., 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen), hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide, and ibuprofen. The concentration of naproxen in the effluent of WWTP from our study was similar to values reported previously from a Canadian WWTP [59], and was markedly higher than concentrations reported in the United States (580 ng/L) [60], Greece (700 ng/L) [61], and China (1–4.5 ng/L) [62]. In contrast, the concentration of hydrochlorothiazide was half of that reported in other regions [63,64]. Naproxen is one of the most prevalent pharmaceutical compounds found in wastewater effluents [60,64,65].

When related to its equivalent pharmaceutical compound, the high levels of ibuprofen were consistent those of the contaminants generated by its metabolite 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen in the WWTPs [66,67]. In this sense, other metabolites or even degraded pharmaceutical substances may exist in water effluents and remain undetected due to their chemical properties, specifically, due to the polar nature of these metabolites. In the case of ibuprofen, the metabolite 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen has a chemical structure similar to that of the initial pharmaceutical compound, with the main difference being a hydroxyl group added in the isopropyl chain that makes it more hydrophilic than ibuprofen. This confers high solubility in water and increases the possibility of further interactions with hydrogen bonds in water (Table 1).

In the early stage of the COVID-19 pandemic, ibuprofen was prescribed as an anti-inflammatory medicine to treat the associated symptoms [6,10]. Carlsson et al. (2006) reported that low concentrations of ibuprofen (∼0.01 μg/L) would increase the environmental risk to aquatic creatures by causing severe chronic toxic effects and reducing their reproduction. Considering the high concentrations of naproxen and ibuprofen in the effluent, WWTPs in Canada may require more advanced treatment methods to further reduce the concentrations in the final sewage before discharging it into the receiving water bodies, to reduce their negative environmental impacts and threats to human health and ecosystems.

Among the pharmaceutical blood regulator contaminants, glyburide and warfarin compounds had the lowest concentrations (< 6 ng/L). These results were similar to those reported in previous studies [64,68]. The concentration of furosemide in the effluent water from this study (425 ng/L) was 1.5-fold higher than that reported from the United States [64], however, was significantly lower than the values detected in Sweden (2500 ng/L) [63] and Greece (15,320 ng/L) [69]. Glipizide, a pharmaceutical compound that is frequently prescribed to treat diabetes, was not detected in our study but was detected in other wastewater effluent analyses in Spain [68,70] and in WWTP effluent in the United States (22–23 ng/L) [71].

BPA, triclocarban, and triclosan were detected in the final effluent at concentrations within comparable ranges of those reported across the world. The detected concentration of BPA was in accordance with some of the values reported in the literature [59,72]. The highest concentrations of the antibacterial compounds triclocarban and triclosan in effluents were reported in the United States (980 ng/L) [60] and South Africa (1890 ng/L) [73], while minimal concentrations of triclocarban and triclosan were detected in our study.

Fig. 1 shows that the wastewater effluent from the Canadian WWTP (Canada [TW]) contained significant amounts of various contaminants including furosemide, naproxen, and 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen, which require more advanced treatment techniques for their removal. These compounds have been used extensively since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic [6,7,10].

Note that the concentrations of PPCP compounds for WW-CA Feb and WW-CA Sep samples were measured in this study, while the concentrations of PPCP compounds from other wastewater treatment plants around the world were obtained from the literature. The detailed information and references for the other studies can be found in Table S1 in the Supplementary Material.

Ibuprofen and naproxen are NSAID prescribed for relief of pain, fever, and inflammation. According to Behera et al. (2011), “It has a low metabolism and a absorption in the human body, most of the administered ibuprofen is excreted via faeces and urine in the form of its parent compound or water-soluble metabolites and consequently released into the environment,” which implies the presence of 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen as a metabolite from its analogous compound ibuprofen [74]. Ibuprofen and naproxen are the most investigated substances within the range of pharmaceutical compounds, due to their availability as over-the-counter products, and have been extensively used by patients across the world since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic [6,7,10]. Their presence in high quantities in WWTP is expected due to their ubiquity.

The removal efficacy of two doses (1 and 10 g/L) of Bio-SBAC and one dose of TWSS-SBAC (1 g/L) as adsorbents in WWTP discharged effluent are shown in Fig. 2 for ibuprofen, 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen, and naproxen. Both SBACs effectively removed these anti-inflammatory compounds. After using 1 g/L dose of Bio-SBAC, the final concentrations of ibuprofen and naproxen were < 10 ng/L, which accounted for 99.8% removal, while for 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen, the final concentration was 185 ng/L, accounting for approximately 91.6% removal. After using the Bio-SBAC dosage of 10 g/L, the final concentration of 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen was 10 ng/L (i.e., 99.5% removal). However, a 1 g/L dose of TWSS-SBAC removed only 70.2% of 2-hydroxy-ibuprofen, 94.2% of ibuprofen and 99.1% of naproxen.

Results from previous studies using different sorbent materials for the removal of ibuprofen and naproxen are shown in Table 3. It is worth noting that all the studies were carried out in simple solute and with only a single contaminant with unrealistically high spiked concentrations [36,37,43,44,75,76]. Considering that, in real effluent from WWTPs, competition with other contaminants and dissolved organic matter reduces the adsorption sites available for contaminants [56–58], to determine the true removal efficiency for an adsorbent material, and obtain accurate and representative results, real wastewater effluent from a WWTP should be used for the adsorption tests.

Removal efficiencies reported in the literature for different adsorbent materials range from 83% to 99% (Table 3) [36,37,43,44,75,76]. The highest reported efficiency was for biochar produced from peanut shell [37]. Notwithstanding the high removal efficiency for biochar, the remaining unadsorbed content of naproxen was 5000,000 ng/L [37], which was remarkably higher than the concentrations of naproxen reported in the real discharged effluent from WWTPs across the world that ranged from below detection limit to 2500 ng/L [59–62]. We conclude that the remaining unremoved amounts of contaminants should be carefully quantified in real effluents discharged from WWTPs to determine the real contaminant-removal efficiency. In contrast, both SBACs removed 99 − 100% of naproxen from the real discharged effluent, showing high sorption removal for the anti-inflammatory drugs.

Fig. 3 shows the effectiveness of Bio-SBAC and TWSS-SBAC for removing blood regulator contaminants from the wastewater effluent. Four compounds (furosemide, gemfibrozil, glyburide, and warfarin) were completely removed by both SBACs at a dose of 1 g/L, while 98 − 99% of the hydrochlorothiazide was removed by both SBACs. Increasing the amount of Bio-SBAC to 10 g/L removed hydrochlorothiazide completely from the wastewater effluent, thus demonstrating a high adsorption capacity for all the blood regulator contaminants.

Table 4 shows different sorbent materials and advanced treatment methods used for removal of furosemide, gemfibrozil, and hydrochlorothiazide. No previous studies on the removal of warfarin and glyburide were found. Pharmaceutical compounds (e.g., furosemide, gemfibrozil, and hydrochlorothiazide) are commonly used, however, research on adsorption and other possible technologies for removing these contaminants from wastewater effluent is scarce. Most studies have been conducted using a stock solution of the contaminant [77–79], while few adsorption studies have used samples of real wastewater from the discharged effluent of a municipal WWTP (Table 4). Nevertheless, Arola et al. (2017) studied the removal of 17 different micropollutants, including furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide, from wastewater effluent using different combinations of nanofiltration (NF) and advanced oxidation (AO) with a membrane bioreactor process (MBR) and found that MBR combined with AO exhibited the highest removal percentage (98–99%) [80]. However, these processes require complicated configurations, high energy input that increases carbon emissions, and frequent maintenance [3,23,31].

Fig. 4 shows the percentages of triclosan, triclocarban, and BPA removal using Bio-SBAC and TWSS-SBAC. The antimicrobial compounds were completely removed with all doses of both SBACs, whereas 99.4–100% of BPA was removed using Bio-SBAC and TWSS-SBAC at 1 g/L dose, and it was completely removed at the 10 g/L dose of Bio-SBAC. These results highlight the high adsorption capacity of SBAC for these contaminants.

BPA is commonly present in a variety of industrial processes as a precursor for epoxy and polycarbonate resins and plastics, and is commonly employed in the production of bottles [81]. Human exposure to BPA is mainly related to wastes generated from manufacturing processes that use BPA, while a secondary cause of exposure is the BPA-based products themselves [22]. Several laboratory experiments have shown that exposure to BPA will induce endocrine disruption in many human organ systems [81].

Table 5 summarises previous studies on the removal of triclosan, triclocarban and BPA. A variety of adsorbent materials such as polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) [82], graphene oxide [83], biochars [38], synthesised materials (i.e., polyvinylpyridine/SiO2/APTMS, polyvinylpyridine/SiO2, and polyvinylpyridine) [84], and commercial adsorbents such as Fullerene C60 [57] have been evaluated for the removal of triclosan, triclocarban, and BPA from stock solutions prepared using water (Table 5). However, there are many limitations and uncertainties with these studies. First, the concentration in most of the cases is high (> 30 mg/L). Second, the concentration of these contaminants in the effluent will remain high (1.5 −45 mg/L) even with a high removal efficiency (> 90%) due to the high initial concentrations. Third, all the studies were conducted by spiking a single contaminant in aqueous solutions using deionised water, without testing real effluents from a WWTP. Moreover, the remaining concentrations employed in the studies reported in Table 5 markedly exceeded the threshold for triclosan in freshwater (0.38 µg/L) according to the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment (CCME) guidelines [85]. Similarly, in the study conducted by Du et al. (2019), the sorbent removal efficiency was high (80–94%); however, the remaining concentrations of BPA were also high, due to the high initial concentrations that ranged from 25 to 500 mg/L. In this scenario the remaining concentration of BPA can reach up to 45 mg/L [82], which is particularly high compared to the 1.75 µg/L of BPA in wastewater effluent discharge proposed by Environment Canada [86].

Another key factor to consider is the high cost of adsorbent materials. For instance, Fullerene C60 costs ∼130,000 USD/kg and commercial activated carbon costs 3.5 − 12 USD/kg [28,87,88], while the production cost for MOFs ranges from 10 to 50 USD/kg [45]. In contrast with these other removal adsorbents materials, SBAC not only effectively removes very low concentrations of triclosan, triclocarban and BPA from the real effluent of the WWTP, it does so at a cost < 1.2 USD/kg SBAC [28,48]. In addition, other co-benefits are associated with the production of SBAC compared to other disposal systems, including reduced greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and global warming potential. Lombardi et al. (2017) estimated that disposal of SS by landfilling, composting, and land application will increase the global warming potential (GWP, as CO2 equivalent) by 1180, 1840, and 1380 kg CO2 eq/tDM, respectively [89].

Triclocarban and triclosan are chemical compounds present in cleaning and washing products, where, due to their high microbicide spectrum, they are used as anti-microbials and fungicides [57,92]. The chemical structure of both the chlorinated compounds is similar; however, triclosan is more soluble in water than triclocarban, which affects its occurrence in the environment [92,93]. They are both found in water, most likely because of incomplete removal of those compounds in WWTP. Both compounds are considered dangerous substances due to their potentially harmful effects on humans and marine ecosystems. In addition, their presence leads to the possibility of evolving antibiotic-resistant strains [92,93]. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has implemented a policy to regulate the utilisation of such chlorinated compounds in personal care products, but they both still appear in WWTP [62].

The results from the adsorption tests in our study demonstrated that SBAC was a highly efficient sorbent material for the removal of various contaminants of PPCPs from the real effluent discharge of WWTPs, and it was highly efficient in comparison with results reported in the literature for other adsorbents. In summary, SBAC can be considered as an excellent sorbent for removing PPCP compounds in low concentrations and reducing the ecotoxicity of unexplored pharmaceutical compounds.

Fig. 5 shows that the FTIR spectra for Bio-SBAC before and after PPCPs sorption exhibited similar patterns. This may be due to the low concentration of PPCPs. However, the FTIR shows SBAC has aromatic functional groups and highly oxidised species, which is supported by the Boehm titration results in Table S2 that identified lactonic (28 mmol/g), carboxylic groups (0.58 mmol/g) and total acidic sites (28.58 mmol/g). Previous studies have suggested that oxygenated functional groups facilitate the adsorption and removal of organic contaminants through hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonding [94–97]. The formation of hydrogen bonds can occur between the H-containing functional groups (i.e., C−H, O−H) on the Bio-SBAC surface and the carbonyl groups (CO) in most PPCPs (Table S3), or between the hydroxyl group (O−H) in the organic molecules (e.g. bisphenol A (BPA) and triclosan) and the carbonyl groups (CO) on Bio-SBAC surfaces [98,99].

Bio-SBAC contains PZC (5.80) and IEP (5.07) and, thus, has a negatively-charged surface, which likely enhances the adsorption of the positively charged of PPCPs, based on their pKa values (Table S3; i.e., BPA, hydrochlorothiazide, triclocarban and triclosan), through electrostatic interactions. Indeed, previous studies have shown that electrostatic interactions serve as the predominate mechanism for the adsorption of BPA onto the negatively-charged biochar surface [96,100]. However, other mechanisms including hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction may contribute to the sorption of other negatively-charged PPCPs (i.e., furosemide, gemfibrozil, glyburide, warfarin, ibuprofen, 2-hydroxyibuprofen, and naproxen) [37,95,97,101]. The BET surface area of Bio-SBAC and TWSS-SBAC is comparable to that of commercial AC (∼700 m2/g) and considerably higher than other adsorbents (<50 m2/g) reported in the literature (Table 5) [51,83,90], illustrating the high adsorption capacity of both SBACs. The high BET surface area is known to contribute to the speeding up of mass diffusion and transfer of PPCP compounds into SBAC internal pores [102], and it is known that diffusion is one of the most limiting factors for the PPCP adsorption process [78]. Enhancing contaminants diffusion is also known to further enhance the hydrophobic interactions, electrostatic interactions, and hydrogen bonding interactions that could be involved in adsorption of PPCPs onto adsorbents [103].

Given the complexity of wastewater effluent, which contains hundreds of contaminants aside from PPCPs, including polybrominated diphenyl ethers, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), heavy metals, and different anions [29,55,104], a systematic investigation to characterise the sorption mechanism of SBAC is recommended. This will help to further improve the surface properties of the sorbent and to optimise the SBAC production process. We expect that this, in turn, will further improve the adsorption capacity of SBAC and reduce its production cost.

The excessive usage of antibiotics, disinfectants, and antibacterial hand-sanitisers and soaps during the COVID-19 pandemic will likely raise the concentration of these PPCPs, along with other emerging pollutants, in the wastewater effluent discharged from WWTPs, thus posing threats to aquatic life and ecosystems [105]. Owing to new and more stringent treatment criteria, energy use (and the associated GHG emissions and other negative environmental impacts) at WWTPs has been predicted to rise by 29–40% [106–108]. The effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, i.e., increased use of PPCPs, have reinforced the need to safely dispose SS and broaden renewable energy technologies worldwide to pursue the lowest negative environmental impacts and GWP [109]. SBAC can be utilised as part of a sustainable waste-to-resources approach for the following: co-producing biofuels and efficient sorbent from SS; stabilising ECs including pharmaceuticals from the precursor SS; removing ECs from WWTP effluent before its discharge to the environment; eliminating the production of solid wastes by wastewater treatment plants; achieving long-term environmental sustainability; mitigating the negative impacts of the pandemic on the discharged wastewater effluent from WWTPs; and reducing the contaminants spread in marine ecosystems.

The SBAC sorbents (Bio-SBAC and TWSS-SBAC) were produced from different sewage sludge precursors to stabilise contaminants and to remove PPCPs from WWTP effluent. To determine the removal efficiency of SBAC for the eleven PPCPs from the wastewater effluent, two dosages of Bio-SBAC (1 and 10 g/L) and one dosage of TWSS-SBAC (1 g/L) were used in the adsorption tests. The remaining concentrations of PPCPs after adsorption were also compared to the worldwide environmental regulatory standards. At the 1 g/L dose, both SBACs completely removed furosemide, gemfibrozil, glyburide, warfarin, triclosan and triclocarban, while the removal efficiency for other compounds ranged from 91.6% to 99.8% for Bio-SBAC and from 70.2% to 99.5% for TWSS-SBAC. Increasing the Bio-SBAC dose to 10 g/L removed all eleven PPCPs from the wastewater effluent to below the detection limit. The results demonstrated that both SBACs are highly efficient sorbents for the removal of various contaminants of PPCPs from the final discharged secondary treatment effluent of WWTPs. We conclude that SBAC can be utilised as a sustainable waste-to-resources approach for producing efficient sorbent from sewage sludge, to stabilise ECs including pharmaceuticals from the precursor sewage sludge, and to improve municipal wastewater effluent water quality impacted by the pandemic COVID-19.
